title: Validating User Input
learningObjectives: Explain why input must be validated before it is trusted.
Check required text fields and basic length constraints.
Validate numeric values against application-defined ranges.
Use simple allowlists for constrained choices.
Combine conversion, validation and clear feedback in a reusable function.

understand.concept: Input validation checks whether received data meets the requirements of a program before it is used. Validation may check presence, type, length, allowed choices and numeric ranges. It should happen close to the point where untrusted data enters the program, and important rules should also be enforced by any trusted server or database layer. A value being syntactically valid does not automatically make it safe or appropriate.
understand.whyItMatters: Validation prevents incorrect records, calculation mistakes and many avoidable application failures. It also improves usability by telling people what needs to be corrected.
understand.analogy: Validation is like an entry checkpoint: it checks whether information meets the stated conditions before allowing it to proceed.
understand.analogyLimit: Validation is not a complete security boundary. Client-side checks can be bypassed, and a valid-looking string may still be dangerous in a different context. Use context-appropriate security controls as well.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Validate required text

Check whether a required field is empty after trimming whitespace. You may also enforce a minimum or maximum length when the task requires it. Do not silently alter data unless normalization is part of the stated rule.

## 2. Validate numeric ranges

First convert the text, handling ValueError. Then check the resulting number against the allowed range. For example, a percentage may need to be between 0 and 100 inclusive.

## 3. Validate choices with an allowlist

When only specific options are permitted, compare the supplied value with a known collection of allowed choices. This is clearer and safer than trying to blacklist every possible unwanted value.

## 4. Reuse validation logic

A function can accept raw text, perform checks and return a clear result. Keep conversion errors distinct from rule violations so callers can give useful feedback.

## 5. Validation is not sanitization or authorization

Validation checks whether data meets expected rules. It does not replace output encoding, parameterized SQL, access control or server-side checks. Never rely only on browser-side validation for important rules.

practise.guidedTask: Validate a size choice against small, medium and large. Then add a numeric check for a percentage between zero and one hundred.
practise.independentTask: Write a registration-data validator for a display name and age. Require a non-empty name of an allowed length, convert age safely and enforce an application-defined range. Return clear error messages.

practise.challenge: Create a reusable validation module with functions for a required text field, a positive quantity and an allowed category. Write tests for valid, invalid, boundary and whitespace-only values.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of input validation?
options: Check that data meets the program's requirements before use
Convert every string to an integer
questions.answer: Check that data meets the program's requirements before use
questions.explanation: Validation checks presence, format, length, allowed values and other application rules.

options: A set of explicitly permitted choices
A list of every possible unwanted value
questions.answer: A set of explicitly permitted choices
questions.explanation: An allowlist defines the values that are accepted.

questions.prompt: When should a numeric range check normally occur?
options: Only after saving to a database
questions.explanation: The program needs a numeric value before it can reliably apply numeric range rules.

questions.prompt: Does browser-side validation alone secure important application data?
options: No, important rules must also be enforced by trusted server-side components
No, because Python cannot validate strings
questions.answer: No, important rules must also be enforced by trusted server-side components
questions.explanation: Client-side checks can be bypassed and do not replace server-side validation or context-specific security controls.

questions.explanation: strip() removes surrounding whitespace, allowing an empty result to identify blank input.
